theme: The strong and the weak; welcome one another
readingInstruction: Read Romans 14:1-15:13. Paul addresses a practical problem in the Roman church: believers who disagree about food and holy days. Notice how Paul handles disagreements on secondary matters, and how he grounds the call to welcome in the example of Christ.
settingTheScene: The Roman church included Jews and Gentiles. Some Jewish believers continued to observe food laws and holy days; some Gentile believers did not. Each group tended to look down on the other. Paul does not tell them to ignore the issue. He gives guidance for how to live together when Christians disagree on matters that Scripture does not settle. This section is very relevant to the church today.
observation: “As for the one who is weak in faith, welcome him, but not to quarrel over opinions” (14:1).
“Each one should be fully convinced in his own mind” (14:5).
“For if we live, we live to the Lord, and if we die, we die to the Lord. So then, whether we live or whether we die, we are the Lord’s” (14:8).
“For the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking but of righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit” (14:17).
“So then let us pursue what makes for peace and for mutual upbuilding” (14:19).
“We who are strong have an obligation to bear with the failings of the weak, and not to please ourselves” (15:1).
“For whatever was written in former days was written for our instruction, that through endurance and through the encouragement of the Scriptures we might have hope” (15:4).
“Therefore welcome one another as Christ has welcomed you, for the glory of God” (15:7).
interpretation:
Paul identifies two groups. The “weak in faith” are those whose consciences are bound on matters like eating only vegetables or keeping special days. The “strong” are those who understand that all foods are clean and every day belongs to the Lord. The surprise is that Paul sides with the strong in belief (14:14, “I am persuaded in the Lord Jesus that nothing is unclean in itself”) but demands that the strong treat the weak with love.

The first rule: “Welcome him.” Do not despise or pass judgment. The one who eats must not despise the one who abstains, and the one who abstains must not pass judgment on the one who eats, for God has welcomed him. “Who are you to pass judgment on the servant of another? It is before his own master that he stands or falls.” Each should be fully convinced in his own mind, acting from faith: “Whatever does not proceed from faith is sin.”

The ground for this tolerance is Christ’s lordship: “None of us lives to himself, and none of us dies to himself. For if we live, we live to the Lord, and if we die, we die to the Lord. So then, whether we live or whether we die, we are the Lord’s. For to this end Christ died and lived again, that he might be Lord both of the dead and of the living.” We will all stand before God’s judgment seat, and each will give an account of himself. That should end our habit of judging others.

The second rule: do not cause others to stumble. “It is good not to eat meat or drink wine or do anything that causes your brother to stumble.” Freedom must be used with love. “The kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking but of righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit.” We should pursue peace and upbuilding. “Do not, for the sake of food, destroy the work of God.”

Chapter 15 gives the pattern: Christ himself. “We who are strong have an obligation to bear with the failings of the weak, and not to please ourselves… For Christ did not please himself.” The example of Christ leads Paul to speak of the Scriptures: written for our instruction, that through endurance and encouragement we might have hope. And he prays for a church with one voice: “May the God of endurance and encouragement grant you to live in such harmony with one another, in accord with Christ Jesus, that together you may with one voice glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.” The command is then repeated and grounded: “Welcome one another as Christ has welcomed you, for the glory of God.” Christ became a servant to the circumcised to confirm the promises, and so that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy.

This does not mean that everything is a matter of opinion. Paul is clear on the gospel, on sin, and on Christ’s resurrection. The category of disputable matters includes issues the Bible does not settle. Wise Christians distinguish essentials, convictions, and preferences. On essentials, unity; on disputable matters, liberty; and in all things, love.

Paul closes with a blessing: “May the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, so that by the power of the Holy Spirit you may abound in hope.”
connection: Leviticus 11 gives the food laws. Mark 7:14-23 shows Jesus declaring all foods clean. Acts 10 shows Peter’s vision. Colossians 2:16-23 deals with food and festival. 1 Corinthians 8 and 10:23-33 deal with food offered to idols. Galatians 5:13-15 speaks of freedom and love. Philippians 2:1-11 calls for the mind of Christ. Psalm 69:9 is quoted in 15:3. Ephesians 4:1-6 speaks of the unity of the Spirit. Psalm 18:49, Deuteronomy 32:43, Psalm 117:1, and Isaiah 11:10 are quoted in 15:9-12. John 17:20-23 is Jesus’ prayer for unity.
application:
Think of a fellow Christian you disagree with on a disputable matter. Welcome them in a concrete way this week.

Ask what freedoms you might lay aside for the sake of someone else’s conscience.

Memorize Romans 15:7 and pray it for your church.
prayerPrompts: Thank Jesus for welcoming you when you were far off.
Ask him to help you welcome someone he has welcomed.
Ask him to give you the mind of Christ toward those who differ.
